issues.legal_issue: A person may be convicted of abetting an offence even when the alleged principal offender is acquitted, if the evidence establishes that the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment.
material_facts: The trial court found that the accused ordered another member of an unlawful assembly to set fire to a hut and that the hut was set on fire in consequence of that abetment.
The appellate court acquitted the person accused of setting the fire because the evidence did not satisfactorily establish that he was the person who did so.
The appellate court nevertheless found that the hut had been set on fire by a member of the unlawful assembly and that the accused had given the order to set it on fire.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for abetting the offence was legally sound because the findings established that the offence was committed in consequence of the accused’s instigation, notwithstanding the alleged principal offender’s acquittal.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 107 and 108 of the Indian Penal Code, abetment includes instigating another to do an act, and an abettor is a person who abets the commission of an offence. Under section 109, where the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor is punishable as provided for the offence; its explanation treats an act as committed in consequence of abetment when it follows the instigation, conspiracy, or aid constituting the abetment. The general proposition in Raja Khan v. Emperor, AIR 1920 Cal. 834, that failure to establish the principal offence precludes abetment liability does not apply where evidence satisfactorily establishes that the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment; Umadasi Dasi v. Emperor, (1924) ILR 52 Cal. 112, recognized that exception.

rule.if: abetment_conviction_appeal and alleged_principal_acquitted and accused_instigated_offence and offence_committed and offence_followed_instigation

predicates.abetment_conviction_appeal: The proceeding challenges a conviction for abetting an offence.
predicates.alleged_principal_acquitted: The person alleged to have personally committed the offence was acquitted.
predicates.accused_instigated_offence: The accused instigated another person to commit the offence.
predicates.offence_committed: The evidence establishes that the offence was in fact committed.
predicates.offence_followed_instigation: The evidence establishes that the offence was committed in consequence of the accused’s instigation.

issues.definition: When an abetment-conviction appeal concerns an acquitted alleged principal, the conviction remains valid if the accused instigated the offence and the offence was committed as a consequence of that instigation.

issues.legal_issue: A court may accept witnesses’ evidence against an accused while rejecting their evidence against another accused when the reasons for rejecting it concern the other accused and do not undermine the evidence against the first accused.
material_facts: The same witnesses gave evidence that the accused ordered the fire to be set and that another person set it.
Some witnesses had omitted or failed to mention that the other person set the fire, but the identified evidentiary infirmities did not apply to their account of the accused’s order.
The appellate court found the witnesses’ evidence consistent against the accused and rejected the allegation against the other person.
issues.conclusion: There was no violation of law or prudence in accepting the witnesses’ evidence against the accused while rejecting it against the alleged principal offender.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that there is no rule of law or prudence requiring a court to accept or reject a witness’s testimony as a whole against all accused persons. Testimony may be accepted against one accused and rejected against another where the court gives reasons and the infirmities relate to the latter allegation.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_appeal and same_witnesses_testified_against_multiple_accused and infirmities_confined_to_other_accused and evidence_consistent_against_accused

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding challenges a criminal conviction based on witness testimony.
predicates.same_witnesses_testified_against_multipl: The same witnesses gave evidence concerning the conduct of more than one accused person.
predicates.infirmities_confined_to_other_accused: The evidentiary weaknesses identified by the court concerned the allegation against another accused and did not undermine the allegation against the accused whose conviction is challenged.
predicates.evidence_consistent_against_accused: The court found the witnesses’ evidence consistent against the accused whose conviction is challenged.

issues.definition: A court may assess testimony differently for different accused when the identified weaknesses are confined to the allegation against one accused and the evidence remains consistent against the other.

issues.legal_issue: A custodial sentence is not excessive where the reviewing court finds that it does not err on the side of severity.
material_facts: The accused’s conviction for abetting the offence carried a sentence of four years’ rigorous imprisonment.
The accused challenged the propriety of the sentence, and the Court found that it was not severe.
issues.conclusion: The sentence was not excessive, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the propriety of the sentence and concluded, without identifying any further sentencing rule or authority, that the sentence did not err on the side of severity.

predicates.criminal_sentence_appeal: The proceeding challenges the severity or propriety of a criminal sentence.
predicates.sentence_does_not_err_on_side_of_severit: The reviewing court finds that the sentence is not unduly severe.

issues.definition: A sentence is not excessive when, in a criminal sentence appeal, the reviewing court finds that it is not unduly severe.
